about.l1: Every number carries a layer badge: Sourced (URL, name, date), Derived (formula) or Assumption (range and rationale).
about.l2: Sources older than 12 months get a “stale” warning. Today: 2026-10-31.
about.l3: Platform reports and real CRM numbers are shown separately; the gap comes from measurement loss and over-reporting.
about.l4: Legal notes are game interpretations, not legal advice.
about.l5: Hidden quality values (offer, creative, landing page) can only be discovered through tests and observation.
about.offline: No external fonts, CDNs or network calls; all data lives in local JSON files.
about.p1: A decision-driven simulation of running marketing and growth for a small SaaS company. The staged funnel, ad channels, measurement loss, test statistics and unit economics follow the logic of real dashboards.
about.p2: The engine is deterministic: the same seed and decisions give the same result. That lets you share seeds, replay saves and ask “what if I had not made this decision” in the outcome analysis.

analysis.score_def: Score = cash + 12 × MRR. A low percentile means luck mattered most; a high one means your decisions were robust.

analysis.top3_note: Impact = difference in cash + 12×MRR when that decision is removed and the run replayed with the same seed.

fact.cac.formula: CAC = (ads + tools + reps + founder hour value) ÷ new paying customers.
fact.cac.title: CAC
fact.cash.formula: Cash = start + revenue + VAT collected − (VAT paid + variable cost + fees + ads + fixed costs + tools + action costs + taxes). Computed by the daily engine step.
fact.cash.title: Cash
fact.ltv.formula: LTV = ARPA × gross margin ÷ monthly churn.
fact.ltv.title: LTV
fact.ltvcac.title: LTV:CAC
fact.marginal.formula: If budget rises 25%: added spend ÷ added customers (expected value from the saturation curve).
fact.marginal.title: Marginal CAC
fact.mrr.title: MRR
fact.payback.title: Payback
fact.reputation.formula: Reputation is a 0–1 simulation variable driven by onboarding quality and events.
fact.reputation.title: Reputation
fact.runway.formula: Runway = cash ÷ average net burn of the last 30 days. Infinite if not burning.
fact.runway.title: Runway

gloss.attribution.def: Deciding which channel gets credit for a conversion. Platform attribution tends to favor itself.
gloss.cac.def: The total sales and marketing cost to win one paying customer.
gloss.churn.def: The share of customers who cancel in a period. It is higher in early months.
gloss.ci.def: The range in which a rate plausibly lies. Little data → wide interval.
gloss.consent.def: A setup that provides aggregated, modelled conversion measurement even when users decline cookies.
gloss.cpa.def: Average spend for one conversion (lead or customer).
gloss.cpc.def: The average amount an advertiser pays for one click: spend divided by clicks.
gloss.cpl.def: Spend ÷ leads. It ignores lead quality; read it alongside CAC.
gloss.cpm.def: The price paid per thousand impressions; usually the primary price unit on Meta.
gloss.ctr.def: Clicks ÷ impressions. A sign of how attractive the creative is.
gloss.fatigue.def: The decay in effect when the same creative is shown repeatedly. Add fresh variants.
gloss.frequency.def: Average times a person saw your ad. High frequency means fatigue and falling CTR.
gloss.funnel.def: The stages from impression to paying customer; each has a conversion rate and the weakest link is the bottleneck.
gloss.gbp.def: The business listing in local search and maps; reviews and completeness influence ranking.
gloss.geo.def: Work to be cited in AI answers; hard to measure and slow to pay off.
gloss.holdout.def: An experiment that turns ads off in some regions and measures the gap; a way to estimate incrementality.
gloss.incrementality.def: Conversions that would not have happened without the ad. Platform reports may count non-incremental ones too.
gloss.is.def: The share of possible impressions you got. Lost share splits into budget (too low) and rank (bid/quality too low).
gloss.learning.def: The period when automated bidding fluctuates until it has enough conversions. Big edits restart it; too little data makes it “learning limited”.
gloss.lookalike.def: A target audience built from users similar to your existing customers.
gloss.ltv.def: The gross profit a customer leaves over their lifetime: ARPA × gross margin ÷ churn.
gloss.ltvcac.def: A health check for unit economics. 3 or more is typical; lower means growth loses money.
gloss.marginal.def: The cost of the extra customer from raising budget one step. Far above average CAC near saturation.
gloss.match.def: Controls which searches a keyword matches: exact (narrow), phrase, broad (widest, leaks most).
gloss.mrr.def: Monthly revenue from active subscriptions. Moves with new, expansion, contraction and churn.
gloss.negative.def: Searches you do not want ads to show for. Cuts irrelevant spend.
gloss.overreport.def: Platforms showing more conversions than real (double counting, view-through attribution, modelling).
gloss.payback.def: Months needed to earn back CAC as gross profit.
gloss.pmax.def: A Google campaign type that auto-allocates across inventory; low transparency and control.
gloss.posterior.def: The belief about a rate after seeing data. P(A>B) is the probability A is truly better than B.
gloss.qs.def: Google’s rating of expected CTR, ad relevance and landing-page experience. When low you pay more for the same position.
gloss.runway.def: How many months the cash lasts at the current burn.
gloss.serverside.def: Sends events from your server instead of the browser to reduce ad-blocker and cookie loss.
gloss.smart.def: Strategies that adjust bids automatically from conversion data. They need data and clean measurement.
goals.title: Goals
google.intro: Campaign > ad group > keyword tree. Numbers are what the platform reports (may differ from your CRM).
google.platform_note: Quality band is shown at campaign level; lost share = impressions missed due to budget or rank.
google.pmax_note: PMax: no ad groups or keywords; conversion-focused strategies only. It allocates by assets and offers lower transparency.
google.starter: Also add an ad group and starter keywords (phrase/exact/brand)
google.terms_day: Report as of day {{n}} (not refreshed until you review again).
google.terms_none: No report yet; reviewing it spends founder hours.
google.type_desc.pmax: Automated delivery across inventory; less control, can capture brand traffic.
google.type_desc.search: Text ads for people searching; high intent, you stay in control.
guide.ab.decide_desc: Ranges separate: B is really better.
guide.ab.wait_desc: Ranges overlap: B may look ahead by chance.
guide.cases.lead: Problems appear during play: a rival cuts prices, tracking breaks, a bad review lands. Some come from your own decisions.
guide.cases.p1: When a case opens on the dashboard, read its symptoms and respond within 14 days.
guide.cases.p2: The right response shortens the effect, the wrong one extends it. Learning mode gives hints.
guide.cases.p3: Raising budget rarely solves the problem; find the cause first.
guide.cases.title: Cases and events
guide.content.lead: What your ad says matters as much as what you spend. In the Studio you choose a main message.
guide.content.p1: Markets respond differently: learning mode gives a directional hint, and testing finds the real answer.
guide.content.p2: If the ad and page share a message, the lead rate rises.
guide.content.p3: In SEO, comparison and local topics bring more leads; on social, customer stories stand out.
guide.content.p4: Do not repeat one topic: returns fall. Bold claims get clicks now but put your account at risk.
guide.content.title: Content and message
guide.example_note: Numbers in the examples are illustrative. In the game they change with market, seed and your decisions.
guide.firstweek.lead: This order is a good start. You do not have to follow it exactly.
guide.firstweek.p1: Keep Tracking setup selected on the start screen: you cannot improve what you cannot measure.
guide.firstweek.p2: Choose Google Ads and Local; leave Meta for later in your first game.
guide.firstweek.p3: On Operations, reserve 2-3 hours a day for sales and 1-2 for onboarding, and turn on auto-reply.
guide.firstweek.p4: On Local, turn on referrals and plan a few hours of content a week.
guide.firstweek.p5: Start the daily budget at about one monthly price; create a new ad in the Studio with a message that fits the market.
guide.firstweek.p6: Advance with +1 week and read the summary. Early data is noisy, so do not change budgets on one day's numbers.
guide.firstweek.title: A sample first week
guide.funnel.lead: Every customer goes through this path. Example: about 5 paying customers from 10,000 impressions.
guide.funnel.log_note: Bars use a log scale so small stages stay visible.
guide.funnel.p1: You pay for clicks, but money only comes at the last step: a trial takes 7-14 days to convert, depending on the market.
guide.funnel.p2: Leads decay while waiting. The later you reply, the lower your chance of reaching them, so auto-reply and sales hours are critical.
guide.funnel.p3: The dashboard funnel shows where you are stuck: fixing the weakest stage pays the most.
guide.funnel.title: Where customers come from: the funnel
guide.goal.lead: You run a small startup selling booking software to barbers and salons for 12 months (90 days in quick mode).
guide.goal.p1: Goal: build recurring revenue (MRR) before cash runs out, with healthy unit economics.
guide.goal.p2: Your target appears in the starting summary and on the dashboard; it varies by market and difficulty.
guide.goal.p3: If you do nothing, almost no customers arrive: you have to create growth.
guide.goal.title: What is the goal?
guide.google.lead: Search ads have high intent but expensive clicks. A row in the Campaigns tab tells you this:
guide.google.p1: Match types: exact is narrow but clean, broad has volume but leaks into irrelevant searches. Start with exact and phrase.
guide.google.p2: Review the search terms report every 2-3 weeks and add irrelevant classes as negatives.
guide.google.p3: Keep brand and core keywords in separate ad groups; mixed groups lower quality score.
guide.google.p4: Smart bidding needs enough conversions; with little data, manual bidding is more predictable.
guide.google.title: Reading the Google Ads screen
guide.intro: Learn the game in 10 minutes. Each section explains one idea with an example; jump anywhere you like.
guide.loop.lead: The game is turn based. Time stands still until you press a button, so think as long as you like.
guide.loop.p1: Confirmed decisions do not apply instantly; they enter today's action queue, and you can Remove them.
guide.loop.p2: If today's founder hours run out, work moves to the next day. Queued jobs run in order.
guide.loop.p3: The +1 day and +1 week buttons in the top bar are on every screen. A summary opens at the end of each week.
guide.loop.title: The game loop
guide.meta.lead: Meta does not capture demand, it creates it. Intent is lower but you reach a wider audience.
guide.meta.p1: Keep a small budget in one ad set: each set needs enough events to learn, and splitting leaves them all limited.
guide.meta.p2: If frequency rises and click rate drops, the creative is fatigued: add a new ad.
guide.meta.p3: Check data sources in Pixel and events; missing data hurts both reporting and learning.
guide.meta.title: Meta ads
guide.mistakes.lead: Avoiding these alone puts you ahead of most players.
guide.mistakes.p2: Starting with broad match and smart bidding, with no negatives.
guide.mistakes.p3: Changing budgets often and resetting learning.
guide.mistakes.p4: Reserving no hours for sales and onboarding: leads decay and customers leave.
guide.mistakes.p5: Scaling on platform reports alone; the CRM may tell a different story.
guide.mistakes.title: Most common mistakes
guide.mock.note1: On/off: pauses the campaign. Do not overuse it, it can reset learning.
guide.mock.note2: Daily budget: the spending cap. Changes above 20% reset learning on smart bidding.
guide.mock.note3: Conversions: what the platform reports, not real customers.
guide.mock.note4: High lost share (rank) means a bid or quality problem, not budget; raising the budget will not help.
guide.msg.page_good: Booking system that grows salon revenue
guide.outcome.healthy: At least half the MRR goal, with healthy economics or runway.
guide.outcome.lead: When time is up you get a result tier. Running out of cash, losing accounts for good, collapsing reputation or burnout end it early.
guide.outcome.p1: The outcome screen shows your key decisions, missed opportunities and the gap between real and reported numbers.
guide.outcome.p2: It compares you with a good bot on the same seed and with other seeds, so you can tell luck from skill.
guide.outcome.stagnant: Revenue did not grow in the last 90 days.
guide.outcome.survived: Still standing, but below your goals.
guide.outcome.title: How the game ends
guide.outcome.won: MRR, customer, LTV:CAC and payback goals were all met.
guide.report.title: Four different numbers for one period
guide.reports.lead: Platforms like to look good. An example comparison for the same period:
guide.reports.p1: Decide using qualified leads and paying customers in the CRM; platform conversions are only directional.
guide.reports.p2: When raising budget, watch marginal CAC, not the average: the next customer always costs more.
guide.reports.p3: Do ads really add customers? The holdout test on the CRM screen measures that.
guide.reports.title: Which number can I trust?
guide.resources.lead: Every decision spends at least one of these. Draining one can end the game.
guide.resources.p1: Cash: ads, fixed costs and new assets come out of it. If it goes below zero, the game ends.
guide.resources.p2: Founder hours: you have about 50 a week, and hours reserved for sales and onboarding come off first. Constant overload leads to burnout.
guide.resources.p3: Reputation: shaped by reviews, onboarding and cold outreach; it drives organic interest and referrals.
guide.resources.p4: Account health: policy violations can suspend Google and Meta accounts; three strikes close them for good.
guide.resources.title: You have four resources
guide.tests.lead: Lines show where the true rate may lie. The further apart they are, the safer the decision.
guide.tests.p1: Small accounts collect data slowly; plan tests for 30-60 days.
guide.tests.p2: Do not pick a winner while the not-enough-data warning shows. A call on 10 visits is close to a coin flip.
guide.tests.p3: When a test ends, assign the winning page on the Edit tab of the Google screen; it does not switch by itself.
guide.tests.title: A/B tests: when to decide
hint.ad_group_focus: An ad group mixes themes. Splitting brand and core keywords into separate groups improves relevance and quality score.
hint.bottleneck.lp: The bottleneck is the landing page: visitors arrive but few become leads. Improve it with an A/B test.
hint.bottleneck.paid: The bottleneck is trial to paid: review onboarding and price.
hint.bottleneck.qualify: The bottleneck is lead quality: possibly the wrong audience or broad match.
hint.bottleneck.trial: The bottleneck is trial start: offer and response speed are critical.
hint.content_topic: In SEO, purchase-intent topics (comparison, local) bring more leads; on social, stories stand out. Repeating a topic lowers returns.
hint.first_day: Set up tracking first, then start with a small budget; you cannot optimize what you cannot measure.
hint.geo: GEO measurement is noisy and delayed; invest small and steadily and expect no quick results.
hint.google: Search ads carry high intent but clicks are expensive. Match type and negatives decide spend quality.
hint.google_strategy: Smart bidding needs enough conversions. With little data, manual CPC can be more predictable.
hint.hours: Work beyond capacity slips to the next day; constantly high load leads to burnout.
hint.local: Free channels do not burn cash but eat your hours. GBP and reviews are strong for local businesses.
hint.marginal_cac: Average CAC may look fine while the next budget increase (marginal CAC) costs far more.
hint.match_types: Broad match brings volume but leaks into irrelevant searches; exact match is narrow but clean.
hint.message.de: In Germany trust and data safety stand out; price messaging is weak. This is a tendency, testing gives the real answer.
hint.message.tr: In Turkey price sensitivity is high, so affordable price stands out. This is a tendency, testing gives the real answer.
hint.message.us: US salon owners tend to respond to revenue growth; price messaging is weak. This is a tendency, testing gives the real answer.
hint.meta: Meta creates demand; intent is lower. Learning needs enough events and few edits.
hint.meta_audience: On a small budget, concentrate spend in one set. Advantage+ and broad audiences give the system room to learn.
hint.pivot: A pivot affects your existing customers; do not pivot without evidence.
hint.platform_vs_crm: Platform conversions can exceed your CRM. Base budget decisions on CRM and incrementality tests.
hint.price: A price rise may cut conversion but lifts LTV; test its effect in isolation.
hint.reset_learning: Big budget, strategy or audience changes can reset learning. Do not tweak too often.
hint.response_time: Responding late to a lead cuts contact rate. Auto-reply and sales hours help.
hint.reviews: Asking happy customers for reviews lifts both reputation and local visibility.
hint.search_terms: The search terms report shows which queries burn money; add irrelevant classes as negatives.
hint.studio: With small samples you can imagine differences. If the intervals overlap, do not decide yet.
hint.tracking: Tracking loss pulls reports down and smart bidding learns from broken data. Consent Mode and server-side tracking reduce the loss.
hint.tracking_health: Tracking health looks low; fix your tags.
history.title: Decision history (ActionLog)
honesty.footer: This is not a forecasting engine; it is an internally consistent and transparent model. All player data is synthetic. Works offline.
honesty.long: This is not a forecasting engine; it is an internally consistent and transparent model. All customer, click and revenue data in the game is synthetic; parameters are labelled as sourced, derived or assumption. Use your own real measurements for real decisions.
honesty.short: This is not a forecasting engine; it is an internally consistent and transparent model.

meta.learning_note: Finishing learning needs enough optimization events within the window; budget/audience/creative edits can reset learning.
meta.messages_note: Messaging ads: leads arrive as conversations; fast replies matter even more.

start.intro: Choose a market, scenario and difficulty; pick your channels and initial setup. Every decision costs founder hours and/or cash.

start.learning_hard: Hard mode never shows hints (even when on).

start.prep.tracking.desc: You cannot learn from ads without measuring conversions.
start.prep_desc: Selected items go to the first-day action queue and spend founder hours and cash. You can edit the queue on the dashboard.
start.title: New game
studio.bold_warn: Bold claims may lift clicks but carry account/policy risk.
studio.intro: Create creative, landing-page and offer variants; discover true quality via A/B tests. Hidden quality values are never shown directly.
studio.low_data_warn: Sample is small: P(A>B) is not reliable. Stopping early can pick the wrong winner.
studio.need_two_lps: A test needs two landing pages; preparing a new one takes a few days.
studio.stat_note: Estimates come from observed counts (Beta-Binomial posterior); with little data the interval is wide and a “not enough data” badge appears.
tip.burnout_risk: You are using almost all founder hours; burnout risk is rising.
tip.frequency: Frequency passed 3 on an ad set; creative fatigue is likely.
tip.hours_idle: You used less than half your founder hours; you could invest time in free channels.
tip.learning_limited: {{n}} campaign(s)/set(s) are “learning limited”; consolidate budget and edit less.
tip.lost_budget: Impression share is lost to budget; consider raising it if efficient.
tip.no_traffic: No traffic yet; open a channel.
tip.platform_vs_crm: Platform conversions are clearly above CRM leads; judge budget by CRM data.
tip.set_tracking: You have not set up tracking yet; conversions may not be measured.
tutorial.advance.title: Advance time
tutorial.advance.why: Queued work only happens when time moves on. Press +1 day in the top bar and watch the queue being processed.
tutorial.channel.title: Open your first channel
tutorial.channel.why: Launch a small exact/phrase Google campaign or start with local channels. Cash is limited and you do not yet know what works.
tutorial.crm.title: Compare platforms with your CRM
tutorial.crm.why: With three weeks of data, check the CRM screen. Platform reports can inflate conversions; your real yardstick is qualified leads and paying customers in the CRM.
tutorial.hours.title: Allocate your hours
tutorial.hours.why: Reserve daily hours for sales and onboarding on the Operations screen. Slow lead response burns lead value quickly, and neglected onboarding raises churn.
tutorial.search_terms.title: Review search terms
tutorial.search_terms.why: Open the search terms report on the Google screen and turn irrelevant queries into negatives. Negatives work less well without reviewing the report.
tutorial.test.title: Start a landing page test
tutorial.test.why: Create a second page in the Studio and start an A/B test. Small accounts need a long time to collect enough data, so do not call a winner early.
tutorial.title: First steps
tutorial.tracking.title: Set up tracking
tutorial.tracking.why: Set up basic tracking on the CRM screen. You cannot optimise what you cannot measure, and smart bidding only learns from the conversions it sees.
tutorial.week.title: Read your first weekly summary
tutorial.week.why: Finish the week. Early data is noisy: do not change budgets on a single day, read the confidence intervals.
weekly.title: Week {{n}} summary
